Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Discuss the epidemiology and risk factors for stress fractures.
Explain the patient history and physical examination findings leading to the diagnosis of a
stress fracture.
Explain which imaging modality to use in the work up of stress fractures.
Delineate between high-risk and low-risk stress fractures.
Review general treatment plan for stress fractures based on high versus low risk.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Stress fractures and stress reactions occur if repetitive microtrauma to a bone exceeds the
capacity of the bone to withstand and repair the microtrauma.


Overview
Stress fractures and stress reactions are on the continuum that is encompassed by the
overarching term bone stress injury in the sports medicine literature.1
Epidemiology
Common in athletes and military personnel with repetitive, high-impact weight-bearing activity
Uncommon in the ribs and upper extremities but occurs with upper-extremity weight-bearing
and repetitive tasks.
Most bony stress injuries occur in the lower extremity, with the tibia and metatarsals the most
common locations.
Stress fractures occur in less than 1% of the general athletic population.
The incidence in running/track athletes may be 10% to 20%.
The rate of recurrence may be approximately 10% in all athletes but as high as 50% in runners.
Female athlete triad and relative energy deficiency in sport are terms used to describe the
interplay of risk factors that increase the risk for stress fractures.

Epidemiology
Bone stress injuries are commonly observed in athletes and military personnel. Initial
research and insight were gathered from the military and then broadened to include
athletes. Most stress fractures occur in the lower extremity, with the tibia and
metatarsals the most common sites. Upper extremity fractures are much less common
but can occur in athletes with upper extremity weightbearing and repetitive throwing
(Video 1).
The female athlete triad has been an accepted entity since 1992. More recently, a similar
phenomenon in males has been found and is termed the male athlete triad. The three
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:31 AM
AAOS | Stress Fractures in Sports Medicine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004086
2/21

components of the triad include low energy availability, reproductive suppression, and
low bone mass.2 In 2014, the International Olympic Committee introduced the term
relative energy deficiency in sport, which emphasizes the central role of low-energy
availability as the causal factor leading to impaired physiologic function in the
musculoskeletal system (low bone mineral density), reproductive system (amenorrhea),
immune system, and cardiovascular system.3
Video 1 Miller T: Stress fractures about the upper extremity, pelvis, and hip, in Kaeding
CC: Problematic stress fractures. Presented at the Annual Meeting of the American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, New Orleans, LA, March 6-10, 2018.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Stress fracture is a fatigue failure of bone that occurs in three stages: crack initiation, crack
propagation, and final fracture.
Stress fractures represent a continuum of severity of bone injury.
Stress fractures result from accumulation of microdamage that occurs with repetitive loading.
Crack initiation: the area of initial stress concentration
Crack propagation: the crack extends if initial microscopic crack is not repaired and repeated
loading of the bone continues
Final fracture: end result of continued fracture


Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
In vivo, bone responds to crack initiation and propagation with a reparative biologic
response that depends on patient age, nutritional status, hormonal status, vascular
supply, biomechanical factors, and possibly genetic predisposition.
A dynamic balance exists between the accumulation of microdamage and the host repair
processes. If microdamage accumulation exceeds the reparative response, the result is a
stress fracture. Any factor that disrupts this dynamic balance may increase the risk for
stress fracture. Any factor that increases tensile, compressive, or torsional forces on a
bone may cause an increase in microdamage accumulation with each loading episode,
especially if applied with an abrupt increase in frequency or intensity. Similarly, any
factor that impairs the reparative biologic response, such as poor vascularity or an
altered hormonal balance, may increase the risk for a stress fracture or an insufficiency
fracture.
Risk Factors
Intrinsic
Female sex
Low body mass index
Low bone mineral density
Low calcium and vitamin D levels
History of previous stress fracture
Foot type
Extrinsic
Training errors: rapid increase in volume or intensity, no days off, lack of cross-training, sport
specialization4
Shoe wear
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:31 AM

4/21


Risk Factors
Stress fractures more often are observed in those with risk factors for suboptimal bone
health. Women are more likely to experience stress fractures than men, possibly related
to the architecture of their bones.5 The female athlete triad has long been accepted as a
reason for increased bone injuries in women with low energy availability and abnormal
menstrual cycles.6 A similar entity, particularly low testosterone levels, is being
researched in males.7 IIn men and women, low energy availability and low sex hormones
are risk factors for stress fractures.2 In addition to the effects of low energy availability
on sex hormones and bone health, relative energy deficiency in sport includes effects on
other body systems, such as metabolic, hematologic, psychologic, cardiovascular,
gastrointestinal, and immunologic systems.3 Additional research on this topic is
necessary.
Extrinsic factors leading to stress fractures usually are related to attempting to do too
much too fast. The bones of individuals who do not give them time to heal the
microarchitectural breakdown can fail.8 A running shoe often is seen as a shock
absorber attenuating the force to the body, and avoiding wearing old, broken-down
running shoes is recommended.
Prevention of stress injuries deserves additional focus and research. Fredericson et al9
found that playing ball sports as a child may help prevent stress fractures later in life.
Nieves et al10 10 reported that drinking milk decreased the risk of stress fractures.
Finally, adequate sleep appears to be protective against stress fractures.11
Injury Classification
Low risk or high risk based on location
Low risk
Cortical bone
Benign natural history
Usually heals with activity and weight-bearing modifications


Injury Classification
Stress fractures generally are classified as low risk or high risk depending on the
location; those with a poor natural history are deemed high risk and usually require
aggressive management. Delayed recognition or undermanagement of high-risk
stress fractures tends to result in fracture progression, nonunion, the need for
surgical management, refracture, and delayed return to sports activity. Other stress
fractures have a more benign natural history and are low risk; these fractures tend
to heal with activity modifications because of compressive forces and adequate
vascularity. Recognizing the class of stress fracture is important in optimizing
management. Over-management of a low-risk stress fracture or undermanagement
of a high-risk stress fracture may result in undue loss of playing time,
deconditioning, and prolonged recovery.
The Kaeding-Miller grading classification system is the only clinical and radiographic
grading system that has been described to date. Table 2 shows three stress fracture
MRI grading systems.5, 12, 13 The system described by Nattiv et al5 differs from that
of Fredericson et al 12 in that periosteal reaction is not a requirement. The two
retrospective studies (Fredericson et al12 and Arendt et al 13) and the one
prospective study (Nattiv et al5) showed a delayed return to sports activity in
SEND FEEDBACK

10/21

patients with a high-grade (grade 4) bone stress injury. This similar finding in all
three studies supports the correlation between MRI grade and the timing of return
to play. Although these classification systems are helpful for research, they also aid
in appropriately gauging the timeline for return to play in the clinical setting.
Knowledge that an athlete’s MRI shows a grade 4 bone stress injury may help set an
approximate timeline for the athlete and coach regarding anticipated time lost from
sports activity. Ideally, surgeons should detect bone stress injuries before they
become high grade so athletes can heal more rapidly with less time lost from sports
activity. (Resource 1).
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Often insidious onset
Worse with prolonged activity
Recent abrupt increase in training mileage or intensity
New footwear
Restrictive eating
Food allergies or intolerance/avoidance
Amenorrhea
Previous stress fractures

Patient History
Stress fractures typically present with an insidious onset of pain but may present with an
acute onset of pain with or without prodrome pain for weeks to months.
A history of a prolonged high-impact activity or a recent abrupt increase in training
frequency or intensity usually is present. Alternatively, a recent change in the type of
training (eg, introduction of interval training) or equipment (eg, a new brand of shoes)
may have occurred. In patients with no history of substantial repetitive loading episodes,

Physical Examination
Point tenderness over the site of possible fracture
Pain with internal rotation of hip if femoral neck stress fracture
Pain with single leg hop test if lower extremity
Current evidence on using a tuning fork for diagnosis is lacking.

Physical Examination
The physical examination may reveal pain with direct palpation or mechanical loading of
the affected site via fulcrum testing of long bones and the single leg hop test.
Laboratory Evaluation
Metabolic bone and nutrition workup, including 25-hydroxyvitamin D level, parathyroid
hormone level, thyroid stimulating hormone level, comprehensive metabolic panel (calcium
level), and complete blood count
May consider sex hormones if amenorrhea in females (estradiol, luteinizing hormone, follicle-
stimulating hormone, human chorionic gonadotropin, and prolactin levels) or sexual
dysfunction in males (free and total testosterone levels)
Consider evaluation for celiac disease if indicated by patient history

Imaging Studies
Radiography
Radiographs rarely positive are unless the injury is severe or chronic.
Typically, radiographic findings lag weeks behind clinical symptoms.
Computed Tomography
Used to identify the presence of a nonunion and to assess the amount of healing in

Associated with a considerable radiation dose.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRIs can be used to identify the bony edema associated with early stress reaction or reveal
the presence of a fracture line (Figures 2 and 3).
MRI is advantageous because it shows the surrounding soft tissues and is most predictive of
time to return to athletic activity.

Bone Scintigraphy
Bone scintigraphy is sensitive in identifying the presence and location of stress fractures.
Do not reveal macroscopic fracture lines in the bone and may be positive for as long as 2 years
after the injury has clinically healed
Ultrasonography
Ultrasonography has been described for the imaging of stress fractures but is used much less
commonly because of its inability to penetrate the cortex.


Ultrasonography
Multiple modalities are available for bone imaging. MRI remains the preferred imaging
modality because of its sensitivity and specificity Radiographs often are obtained initially
to assess for visible fracture or periosteal reaction; however, they often appear normal.
Although some insurance plans have been known to require two radiographs obtained 7
to 10 days apart, the next step after initial radiography ideally is MRI. CT, bone
scintigraphy, and ultrasonography are reasonable alternatives but are associated with
limitations.


Nonsurgical Management
Management must alter the biomechanical and biologic environment to allow the
reparative processes to overcome the accumulation of microdamage at the fracture site.
A holistic approach is required to optimize healing potential. An athlete’s biologic bone-
healing capacity should be evaluated, including review of nutritional, hormonal,
psychological, biomechanical, and medication status; screening for the female athlete
triad and relative energy deficiency in sport also should be performed. Nutritional
support with appropriate caloric intake along with calcium and vitamin D
supplementation may be necessary to achieve healing and prevent recurrence.
The fracture site also must be protected from future strain episodes via relative or
absolute rest, bracing, technique modification, or surgical fixation (Figure 4).

severity according to the Kaeding-Miller classification system. (Reproduced with
permission from Rockwood and Green’s Fractures in Adults, ed 9. Philadelphia, PA, Wolters
Kluwer, 2018.)
Relative rest involves decreasing the frequency or magnitude of strain episodes at the
stress fracture site by modifying the training volume (intensity, duration, and frequency),
technique, and equipment; by using a brace or orthosis; by cross-training. Absolute rest
removes all strain episodes from the fracture site. This rest often is achieved by having
the athlete bear no weight, use crutches, and undergo immobilization.

Assessment of biomechanical risk factors, such as malalignment, should be performed
to determine the risk of recurrence. This may include leg-length discrepancy, cavus or
planus foot type, increased hip adduction, and/or rearfoot eversion. Video analyses of
running gait and throwing are ideal for determining form and technique abnormalities.
The use of biophysical enhancement technologies in patients with a stress fracture, such
as pulsed ultrasonography and electrical stimulation, has not been shown to be a major
factor in healing acute stress injuries.
Biphosphonates, teriparatide, and transdermal estrogens are evolving treatment options
for promotion of bone healing that should be considered in certain situations, such as
nonunion of a fracture in a patient with osteoporosis after appropriate treatment.
Surgical Management
Indications
High-risk stress fractures
Nonunion
Rehabilitation
Physical therapy may be necessary if atrophy or weakness occurs secondary to limited/non–
weight-bearing status.
Core strengthening is useful in alignment and controlling the load through the lower
extremity/kinetic chain.
Strength, flexibility, and gait/running analyses often are necessary to help prevent recurrence
of stress fractures.
